title: About
text:
I’m Stéphane Cuenat, a software architect based in Porrentruy, in the Swiss Jura.
By day I’m Principal Software Architect at Mastercam, where I work on the SDKs and on bringing AI into CAM software, the tools that turn a 3D model into instructions for a machine. Before that I led development and research teams, and early in my career I had the chance to take part in SwissCube, Switzerland’s first satellite.
I hold a PhD in computer science from FEMTO-ST and the Université de Franche-Comté. My research combined deep learning and digital holography to measure position in 3D with sub-micrometer accuracy, using small transformer networks fast enough to run on a CPU. I still write research papers with FEMTO-ST, especially with Raphaël Couturier.
This site is where I think in public. I write about what AI really changes and what it doesn’t: learning and the time it takes, why we need less data rather than more, what machines can and can’t rebuild, and what wisdom means next to intelligence. Some pieces are short essays from my newsletter AI, Honestly. Others are longer working papers.
I’m interested in ideas more than hype, so challenges and counter-arguments are always welcome.
How I write. The questions, ideas and arguments here are mine, and so is the responsibility for them. But I don’t write alone: I use AI to challenge my ideas, shape them, tighten the text and help with code and experiments. It would be odd to write about AI honestly and hide that.
Opinions here are my own and not those of my employer.
This site counts visits anonymously with GoatCounter: no cookies, no personal data, no tracking across sites.

title: Show What Changed, Not the Data
text:
Working paper, September 2026. Download the PDF. Continued in What a Quiet Screen Cannot See, which answers a reader’s objection.
Abstract. Many organisations use AI to produce more: more metrics, more reports, more dashboards. And we end up looking at data. This paper argues that data is not what we need. A simple lesson from mathematics shows why more numbers explain the past better but guide decisions worse. The paper then argues that summarising data well and finding the rules behind it are the same task, and that the result is a shape: a small description of how a system works. Its main proposal is that the dashboard should show neither the data nor the shape, but the difference between today’s shape and the previous one: what changed in our understanding. A simulated case based on the telemetry of an AI copilot shows the gain.

title: Show What Changed, Not the Data
text:
1. The dashboard problem
AI makes it cheap to produce information, so we produce more of it: more reports, more summaries, more tiles on dashboards that already have forty. But reading still takes as long as it always did. Human attention is the real limit.
And so we end up looking at data. The screen fills with numbers, and understanding is left to the reader. We measure more than ever, yet decisions do not feel better informed. This paper argues that data is not what we need, and that producing more of it is not progress. What we need is understanding and, above all, knowing when our understanding has to change.

title: Show What Changed, Not the Data
section: 2. The curve that fits too well
text:
2. The curve that fits too well
Imagine we have some noisy measurements and want to draw a curve through them. A common tool is a polynomial, a sum of terms:

p(x) = a_0 + a_1 x + a_2 x^2 + \dots + a_n x^n

The more terms we add, the closer the curve gets to each point. With enough terms, it passes through all of them. That looks perfect, but it is not. Between the points, the curve swings wildly (Figure 1). It has learned the noise, not the real shape.



Figure 1. Sixteen noisy measurements. The curve with 15 terms (red) hits every point but swings far away between them. The simple curve with 3 terms (blue) misses some points but follows the real shape. All figures in this paper use simulated data.


A dashboard does the same thing, except that the fitting happens in people’s heads. Show someone forty indicators and they will find a story: this dip was caused by that event. With enough indicators, some story always fits the past. The reader becomes the curve with too many terms. That is why every extra number has a cost, even when it is correct.

title: Show What Changed, Not the Data
section: 3. Explaining the past vs. predicting the future
text:
3. Explaining the past vs. predicting the future
Figure 2 shows the trade-off. Adding terms always improves the fit to past data. But the ability to predict new cases improves only up to a point, and then gets much worse. The best result comes from a small number of terms.



Figure 2. As terms are added, the fit to past data keeps improving (grey). Prediction of new data (blue) is best with 3 terms, then gets much worse.


The same holds for dashboards. Three well-chosen numbers may look less complete than thirty, but they guide action better. Being complete and being accurate are not the same goal.

title: Show What Changed, Not the Data
text:
4. Lots of data, few numbers
This does not mean we should collect less data. To find the few right numbers, we often need many measurements. The real question is who does the summarising. In Figure 3, 120 measurements are reduced to six numbers that describe the whole surface, even where nothing was measured. Machines should handle the volume; people should receive the result.



Figure 3. 120 measurements (red) summarised by a surface described by only six numbers (blue).


So the best use of AI here is not to produce more, but to reduce: to take large, messy data and return the few numbers that explain it, with an honest statement of how certain it is (Figure 4). Three simple tests help decide what to keep:

Decision test. Would this change what anyone does? If not, remove it.
Prediction test. Does it help predict what comes next, or does it only describe the past?
Simplicity test. Could we say the same with fewer numbers? If so, the extra ones are noise.




Figure 4. The information funnel. Each step should be smaller than the one before, so that what reaches a person is small enough to act on.

title: Show What Changed, Not the Data
text:
5. Summarising is discovering
A curve shows the shape of the data, but not why it has that shape. For that, we need rules. One might think that finding rules is a separate step that comes after summarising. It is not. It is the same task.
Here is why. The shortest way to describe a set of data has two parts: a rule, plus the exceptions the rule does not explain.

\text{data} = \text{rule} + \text{exceptions}

The best summary keeps both parts as short as possible, and the rule that achieves this is the best explanation of the data. Put simply: the raw data is a file, a summary is a compressed file, and a rule is the recipe that produces the file.
History shows this well. Tycho Brahe spent decades recording the positions of the planets. Kepler summarised his tables in three short laws. Newton then discovered gravity, not from Tycho’s raw tables, but from Kepler’s three laws. The rule was found in the summary, not in the raw data.



Figure 5. Top: from data, to summary, to rule. Bottom: the same idea as a method. Summarising and finding rules form a loop, driven by what the rule still misses. Rules are tested in practice before they are trusted.


Modern AI can work the same way. First, a neural network learns to summarise the data into a few variables. Then a second method searches those few variables for simple equations. Researchers have used this to rediscover known laws of physics from raw measurements, even from video. So to the question “how would AI find the rules?”, the answer is: summarise first, then look for rules in the summary.
Three cautions apply:

Keep what predicts, not what is big. A summary that keeps only the largest effects can throw away a small signal that holds the rule.
It is a loop, not a straight line. To summarise well, you need an idea of the rule; to find the rule, you need a good summary. So we go round: summarise, guess a rule, look at what it misses, summarise again.
A pattern is not a cause. A rule found in past data may break once people act on it. As Goodhart’s law puts it, when a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure. Rules must be tested in practice.

title: Show What Changed, Not the Data
text:
6. The shape of a system
We can now name what this work produces. Call it the shape of the system: the smallest description that explains its data. It has three layers.

Structure: what kind of system it is. One group or several? Does it repeat in cycles, or drift?
Rules: how it works. What drives what, and how strongly.
Scale: a few key numbers that say how much.

Structure deserves a word, because averages cannot see it. In Figure 6, three datasets have exactly the same average and spread, yet one is a cloud, one is a loop and one is two loops. A process that repeats and a process that drifts are very different, even if their averages match. A branch of mathematics called topological data analysis detects such structure and describes it with a few numbers: how many groups, how many loops.



Figure 6. Three datasets with the same average and spread. Standard statistics cannot tell them apart, but their shapes are completely different: no loop, one loop, two loops.


In practice, a shape fits on a small card of a few dozen numbers. It is our current understanding of the system. It is far smaller than the data, and far more useful.

title: Show What Changed, Not the Data
section: 7. Show what changed, not what is
text:
7. Show what changed, not what is
Here is the central idea of this paper. Data arrives all the time, so the shape is updated regularly, for example every week. Most weeks, the new shape is almost the same as the old one: the system behaves as we understand it. Occasionally the shape changes: a rule stops holding, a new group appears, a key number moves.
The dashboard should show exactly that: the difference between the new shape and the previous one.

\text{dashboard} = \text{shape}(\text{this week}) - \text{shape}(\text{last week})

Mathematicians call this a finite difference. The dashboard then shows neither the data nor even the shape, but how our understanding has changed (Figure 7).



Figure 7. Illustrative. Bottom: the raw data, used as evidence and never shown. Middle: the shape, our understanding, updated each week. Top: the difference between consecutive shapes. This is the dashboard, and it stays empty until the shape changes.


This gives three layers, each with its own role. Data is evidence: it is kept, but rarely shown. The shape is understanding: anyone can consult it when they want to know how the system works. The difference is news: it is the only thing that needs attention.
It also separates two kinds of surprise. A surprise within the shape is a single measurement that does not fit the rules: an unusual request, a bad day. The system handles those itself. A change of the shape means the rules themselves have moved. That is what people need to know.
Most of the time, the difference is zero and the dashboard is empty. That is the goal, not a flaw. An empty dashboard means our understanding still holds.

title: Show What Changed, Not the Data
text:
8. Five cautions for taking differences
The idea is simple, but taking differences has well-known traps. Each has a simple answer.

Differences amplify noise. Subtracting two noisy numbers gives an even noisier one. If shapes are compared too often, random swings look like change. The time step must be long enough for the shape to be measured reliably. Mathematicians face the same choice when picking the step of a finite difference.
Subtract the change you already expect. If usage grows every week, the raw difference shows growth every week. That is not news. The dashboard should show the difference minus what the rules predicted: the change of the change.
Compare like with like. Two shapes can only be subtracted if they are described in the same terms. If the summary is rebuilt from scratch each time, its terms may shift meaning. Keep the frame fixed, or align the shapes before comparing.
Look at more than one time scale. A slow drift can be too small to notice from one week to the next and still add up to a large change. Compare the shape not only with last week, but also with a fixed reference, such as last quarter.
Weigh change by what it affects. A small change near a decision point can matter more than a large one elsewhere. Only changes large enough to affect a decision should appear, and the people who own the decisions, not the analysts, should decide what counts as large enough.

title: Show What Changed, Not the Data
text:
9. Data becomes evidence
In this view, data changes role. It is no longer something to look at. It is evidence: used to build the shape, to check it, and to show when it must change. Three ideas explain what kind of data is worth having.
Information is surprise. A number we already expected tells us nothing new. Only the gap between what happened and what the shape predicted carries information. A leading theory in brain science suggests the brain works in a similar way: it passes on mainly what differs from expectation.
Measure where things change. A rule tells us how things evolve; given a starting point, it can rebuild the rest. So data is needed mainly where the shape is unsure or changing. In Figure 8, the same 13 measurements, placed where the curve changes, give an error six times smaller. In practice we do not know in advance where things change, so we find out step by step: measure a little everywhere, then more where the surprises are.



Figure 8. Thirteen measurements placed evenly (top) or where the curve changes (bottom). The second version follows the curve much more closely with the same number of points.


Data is worth what it changes. A measurement is valuable only if it could change a decision. When the choice is already clear, more data adds nothing (Figure 9). A good shape makes choices clearer, and so reduces how much data we need.



Figure 9. How much a new measurement is worth, depending on how close we are to a decision. It matters most near the tipping point, and less when the model is confident.


In practice: collect a little everywhere, and much more where the shape is changing. Keep the raw data in an archive for the day a new rule is needed. Show it only when someone asks.

title: Show What Changed, Not the Data
text:
10. What replaces the dashboard
What people see becomes small. The system produces three things:

A change notice, when the shape changes in a way that matters: what changed, by how much, why it matters and what to do.
A heartbeat, each period: “shape checked on this week’s data, no material change.” Without it, an empty dashboard is ambiguous, because a broken system is empty too.
The shape itself, on demand, for anyone who wants to understand the system or ask a question.

Dashboards also serve other purposes: a shared picture for the team, accountability, audits and trust. These needs remain, and this approach serves them better. The shape is the shared picture. The history of changes is the audit trail. The heartbeat makes “nothing changed” a clear, checkable statement rather than a feeling.
There are real risks. People who stop watching can lose their feel for the system, and a system cannot see a change its shape does not describe. Three safeguards help: review the shape itself regularly; let people explore the raw data from time to time, looking for what the shape misses; and keep people, not the system, responsible for the limits and the decisions.
Building such a system follows a short method:

Start from decisions. List the decisions people actually make.
Compress into a shape that predicts. Keep what predicts, and let each rule know its own noise.
Fix the frame, so that shapes can be compared over time.
Choose the step, long enough to measure the shape reliably.
Compute the difference minus the expected change, against last period and against a fixed reference.
Keep only material changes, publish them with a heartbeat, and archive the data.

title: Show What Changed, Not the Data
text:
11. A simulated case: copilot telemetry
To make this concrete, we simulated 90 days of telemetry from an AI copilot with five agents: search, code, summarise, translate and email. Each request records its language (English, German, French or Italian), the agent, the function used, the request length and the response time. Usage grows slowly and drops at weekends, and a new export function is gradually replacing the older draft function. Response times also move up and down each day for everyone, because the servers are shared.
We hid two real problems. From day 45, the translate agent starts slowing down very gradually, by 0.2% per day. On day 60, the code agent suddenly becomes 25% slower, for German requests only. In total, the simulation produces 1.6 million requests and about 10 million numbers.
The usual dashboard. A typical dashboard shows 24 tiles: requests per language and per agent, response time per agent, and how often each function is used (Figure 10). Each tile is flagged when it leaves its normal range. Over the last 60 days, the tiles raise 106 flags. Normal growth and the new export function look like anomalies. Each real problem is flagged just once, both on day 74 during a server spike, with nothing to set them apart from the 104 false flags. Neither cause is named. This baseline is deliberately simple. A careful analyst would adjust each tile for weekends and growth, and remove most of the false flags. But the two real problems would still be hidden in the daily server swings, and no tile would name the cause.



Figure 10. The usual dashboard: 24 tiles over 90 days. Red dots mark days outside the normal range: 106 flags, almost all false. The dotted line marks day 60.


The shape. The system first summarises the raw requests into 7,200 small groups, one per day, agent, language and request length. From this summary it learns the rules: weekdays bring four times more requests than weekends; usage grows by about 0.3% per day; export is steadily replacing draft; and response time grows with the square root of request length (learned value 0.54, against 0.5 used to create the data). Each week, it then describes the copilot with a shape card of 33 numbers: overall volume, the language mix, the speed of each agent in each language (after removing the effect of request length and the shared server swings), and the share of each function within its agent. Twelve weeks of shapes amount to fewer than 400 numbers, instead of 10 million.
The dashboard. Figure 11 shows the difference between each week’s shape and the previous one. On the left is the raw difference: many cells light up week after week, because volume grows and export replaces draft. On the right is the difference minus the expected change, keeping only material changes (5% for speed and volume, two percentage points for usage). These thresholds are not technical choices; they should be set by the people who own the decisions, for example the team responsible for response times. For twelve weeks, the whole dashboard is empty except for one line: code agent, German. The notice appears at the end of week 9, two days after the problem began, and names the cause. It appears again in week 10, because the week-9 shape contained only three days of the problem. After that, the new speed is part of the shape, and the dashboard is quiet again.



Figure 11. The dashboard as a difference of shapes, over 12 weeks. Left: the raw week-to-week difference of the 33 numbers in the shape card. Right: the difference minus the expected change, keeping only material changes. One line remains: code agent, German, weeks 9 and 10.


The slow drift. The translate slowdown never moves more than 1.7% from one week to the next, so it never appears on the weekly dashboard. Compared with a fixed reference shape (weeks 1 to 6), it crosses the 5% line in week 12 and is reported (Figure 12). This is the fourth caution at work.



Figure 12. The slow drift of the translate agent. Week-to-week changes (bars) stay small. The change compared with a fixed reference shape (line) keeps growing and crosses the materiality line in week 12.


The time step. If shapes are compared every day instead of every week, noise alone produces 51 speed changes above 5% in the first 59 days, before anything real has happened. Weekly comparison produces none. This is the first caution at work.
A limit. We hid both problems along dimensions the shape card tracks: agent and language. A problem along a dimension it does not track, such as device type, would not appear at all. This is the real limit of the approach, and the reason why the shape itself must be reviewed, and the raw data explored from time to time (Section 10).

Table 1. The two approaches on the same simulated data. The dashboard figures cover 90 days, the shapes 12 full weeks. The 3 notices are two for the sudden problem (weeks 9 and 10) and one for the drift.

Two lessons came from building the case itself. Our first summary dropped request length, and the length rule could not be found: the system learned 0.33 instead of 0.5. A summary must keep what predicts. An early version also ignored that weekends have fewer requests, which makes usage noisier on those days; it raised ten false alarms. A rule must know its own noise. Both are the loop of Section 5 at work: the surprises showed us what the shape was missing.
The gain is clear. People no longer read data. They read, at most, a few lines about what changed in the system, and a weekly confirmation that nothing else did. The data is still there, used as evidence rather than shown as content.

title: Show What Changed, Not the Data
text:
12. Conclusion
We set out from a simple observation: AI makes it easy to produce more, and we end up looking at data. Data is not what we need. What we need is understanding, and the ability to notice when it must change. Summarising data well and finding the rules behind it are one task, and its result is a shape. The dashboard, finally, should be the difference between shapes: an empty page on most days, and a few precise lines when our understanding of the world has to move. We do not need more data on more screens. We need a good shape, a careful way of measuring how it changes, and the humility to keep checking that it still holds.

title: What a Quiet Screen Cannot See
text:
Essay, October 2026. A follow-up to Show What Changed, Not the Data. The simulation code is here: sim.py, figs.py.
In short. My last essay argued that a dashboard should show only how our understanding of a system has changed, so that most weeks it is empty. A reader pointed out the weak spot: if something goes wrong in a place our understanding does not cover, the screen stays quiet while the system fails. He is right, and this essay takes the objection seriously. An empty dashboard can mean two different things, nothing changed or something changed where we are not looking, and the dashboard alone cannot tell them apart. But the data can. Every summary leaves something unexplained, and when the world changes in a direction the summary does not cover, that leftover part grows. Watching it costs very little, and it turns a silent blind spot into a warning.

title: What a Quiet Screen Cannot See
text:
1. The objection
After I published the first essay, a reader named Ronald wrote a comment that I have been thinking about since. He liked the idea and compared it to how the brain works: it does not process everything it receives, it predicts what should happen and reacts only to the difference. An empty dashboard, he said, is like a well-adapted organism with nothing to react to.
Then he added the caveat. The dashboard has a built-in blind spot. If something goes wrong outside what the shape describes, the screen stays silent while the system fails without a sound.
I had mentioned this limit at the end of the paper, in one paragraph. That was not enough. The whole proposal rests on one promise: if the screen is empty, you can look away. If an empty screen can also mean “something is breaking where I cannot see”, then the promise is broken, and the old crowded dashboard starts to look safer. So the question deserves a full answer: when can we trust silence?

title: What a Quiet Screen Cannot See
text:
2. Two silences
Imagine two weeks in which the dashboard shows nothing.
In the first week, nothing changed. The system behaved as our shape (our compact description of how it works) said it would. Silence is good news.
In the second week, something did change, but in a direction the shape does not describe. Perhaps one type of device became slow, and the shape does not track devices. The shape is recomputed, it looks the same as last week, the difference is zero, and the screen is empty. Silence is now bad news, and it looks exactly like the good news.
In the first essay I added a heartbeat: a weekly line saying “shape checked on this week’s data, no material change.” It solves a real problem. Without it, a broken pipeline and a healthy system both produce an empty screen. But the heartbeat only proves that the system is checking. It does not prove that the system can see the change that matters. In the second week, the heartbeat is sent, it is true, and it is useless.

title: What a Quiet Screen Cannot See
section: 3. The geometry of a blind spot
text:
3. The geometry of a blind spot
It helps to picture this. The shape is a small set of numbers: for example the speed of each agent in each language, after removing the effect of request length and the daily ups and downs of the shared servers. Think of each number as one direction in which the system can move. Together, these directions form the space that the shape describes.
Any real change in the system is an arrow. Part of that arrow points along the directions the shape describes; that part moves the shape and reaches the dashboard. The rest points elsewhere; it moves nothing the shape measures, so the difference of shapes does not see it at all (Figure 1).



Figure 1. A change in the system splits into two parts. The part along what the shape describes moves the shape card and can reach the dashboard. The part outside it is invisible, however large. A large real change can still show only a small shadow on the dashboard, too small to report.


Mathematicians call the visible part a projection. The dashboard of the first essay sees only the projection of each change onto the shape. This is not a flaw of one dashboard; it is true of every model, every summary and every set of indicators. You can only report a change in the words you have. A thermometer cannot tell you that the room is on fire if the fire has not yet warmed the air near it.
The danger is not only that some changes are invisible. It is that the shape will often explain them away. If a change looks, from inside the shape, like something the shape already expects, such as noise or a known swing, the shape will absorb it into that category without complaint.

title: What a Quiet Screen Cannot See
text:
4. The setup
To see how this happens, I reused the simulated AI copilot from the first essay: five agents (search, code, summarise, translate, email), four languages (English, German, French, Italian), request lengths, slow growth, quiet weekends, and response times that rise and fall each day for everyone because the servers are shared. Over 12 weeks the simulation produces about 2.2 million requests.
One thing is new. Each request now also records three fields the shape card does not use: the device (web browser, desktop app or iOS app), the region and the customer’s plan. This is realistic. Telemetry usually records far more fields than any summary uses.
The shape card is the same as before: the speed of each agent in each language, after removing the effect of request length and the shared daily swings. It learns the length rule correctly (exponent 0.50, the value used to create the data) and it is quiet for seven weeks, as it should be.
Then, on the Wednesday of week 8, requests from the iOS app become 15% slower, for every agent and every language. Perhaps an app update changed how requests are packed. iOS is 15% of all traffic.

title: What a Quiet Screen Cannot See
text:
5. Why the shape stays quiet
The shape card never moves. Over the twelve weeks, the largest change in any of its numbers is 2.6% from one week to the next, and 2.5% compared with the reference weeks. The materiality line is 5%. The dashboard is empty for all twelve weeks, and twelve heartbeats report “no material change” (Figure 2).
The reason is instructive. The slowdown hits every agent and every language equally, because iOS users are spread evenly across them. So the relative speeds that the shape card tracks do not change at all. What does change is the overall level: on average, all requests are about 2% slower. But the shape was built to treat changes in the overall level as server swings, because the servers really do swing, by about 5% from day to day. A step of 2% inside daily swings of 5% looks like one more swing. Look at the top panel of Figure 2: the 7-day average wandered just as much in weeks 3 and 4, when nothing was wrong.



Figure 2. Top: the shared daily level, which the shape treats as server swings. The iOS slowdown adds a step of about 2% from day 51, inside daily swings of about 5%. It is indistinguishable from earlier wandering. Bottom: the dashboard. The largest change in the shape card never comes close to the 5% line.


This is the worst kind of blind spot. The shape does not ignore the problem. It explains it, with full confidence and the wrong explanation. A 15% slowdown for one in seven users becomes “the servers had a slightly slow fortnight”.
The fourth caution of the first essay, comparing against a fixed reference and not only against last week, does not help here either. That caution catches slow changes along the directions the shape describes. This change is not slow; it is sideways.

title: What a Quiet Screen Cannot See
text:
6. The leftover part
The way out comes from an idea that was already at the centre of the first essay. The shortest description of a set of data has two parts:

\text{data} = \text{rule} + \text{exceptions}

The shape is the rule. The exceptions are everything the rule does not explain: for each small group of requests, the gap between the speed the shape predicts and the speed that was actually measured.
When the shape is right, the exceptions are pure noise. They have a typical size, which we can measure in quiet weeks, and they have no structure: you cannot predict them from anything.
When the world changes in a direction the shape does not describe, the change has to go somewhere. It cannot go into the shape, so it goes into the exceptions. In the language of Figure 1, the unseen part of the arrow is not lost; it lands in the leftover part. The exceptions get bigger, and they start to have a pattern.
So the shape needs a second, very simple monitor next to the dashboard. It asks two questions each week.

Are the exceptions bigger than usual? If the rule still holds, the leftover part should be as large as it was in quiet weeks, no larger.
Can anything explain them? For each recorded field that the shape does not use, check how much of the exceptions it explains. If the shape still holds, the answer should be: almost nothing.

The first question tells us that the shape is wearing out. The second tells us where.

title: What a Quiet Screen Cannot See
text:
7. What the exceptions show
Figure 3 shows the first question in the simulation. The size of the exceptions is measured relative to the first six weeks, so 1 means “usual”. For seven weeks it stays within about 1% of 1. In week 8, it jumps to 1.18, then settles between 1.30 and 1.37. With a materiality line at +10%, the monitor raises a notice at the end of week 8, five days after the problem began. The shape card, for the same weeks, still says nothing has changed.



Figure 3. The size of the exceptions, relative to the first six weeks. It stays at 1 until the iOS problem starts, then crosses the +10% line at the end of week 8. The dashed line shows what happens once the shape learns device type: the exceptions return to their usual size.


There is something important here. This first check does not need the device field at all. It only needs to know that the rule now explains the data less well than it used to. Even if the device were never recorded, we would know that the shape no longer fits, without knowing why. That alone is worth a lot: it changes the heartbeat from “no change” to “no change in the shape, but the shape fits worse than usual”. That is a very different message, and a much more honest one.
Figure 4 shows the second question. Before the problem, the device field explains only 1 to 2% of the exceptions. That small part is real: iOS requests were always about 3% slower, a constant difference the shape never learned. After week 8, the device field explains 18 to 19% of the exceptions. Region and plan stay below 1% throughout.



Figure 4. How much of the exceptions each recorded field explains. Device type jumps from 1–2% to almost 20% when the iOS problem starts. Region and plan stay close to zero. The monitor does not only say that something is wrong; it says where to look.


So the notice can say something precise: the shape fits worse than usual, and most of what it cannot explain is linked to device type; iOS requests are about 15% slower than the shape expects. That is almost the full diagnosis, found by a monitor that has no idea what an iOS app is.

title: What a Quiet Screen Cannot See
text:
8. The shape learns
What happens next is the loop from the first essay: summarise, look at what the rule misses, summarise again. The notice tells us the shape is missing a dimension. So we add it: the shape card gains two numbers, the speed of the desktop app and of the iOS app relative to the web.
With those two numbers, the shape learns that iOS was about 3% slower than the web before week 8 and about 18% slower after, which matches the 15% slowdown we hid. The exceptions return to their usual size (the dashed line in Figure 3). The screen becomes quiet again, and this time the silence is justified.
This is how a shape should grow: not by adding every field “just in case”, which brings back the crowded dashboard and the curve with too many terms, but by adding a dimension when the exceptions prove that it is needed. The leftover part is not waste. It is where the next rule comes from. Kepler gave up circular orbits because of an eight-arcminute gap in the orbit of Mars that circles could not explain.

title: What a Quiet Screen Cannot See
section: 9. Predictive coding has the same problem
text:
9. Predictive coding has the same problem
Ronald’s comparison with the brain is a good one, and it goes further than he said. A well-known theory in neuroscience, predictive coding, proposes that the brain constantly predicts what its senses will report, and passes on mainly the difference between prediction and reality. This is exactly a dashboard of differences. And the brain has exactly the same blind spot.
The most famous demonstration is an experiment by Simons and Chabris. Viewers are asked to count the passes in a video of people throwing a basketball. Halfway through, a person in a gorilla suit walks through the scene. Roughly half of the viewers do not notice the gorilla at all. They were not looking in the wrong place; the gorilla walked through the middle of the screen. Their model of the task simply had no slot for gorillas.
So how does the brain survive in a world full of gorillas? One influential answer, from Yu and Dayan, is that the brain tracks two kinds of uncertainty. Expected uncertainty is the normal noise of a familiar situation: we know the world is a bit unpredictable and we do not react to every small surprise. Unexpected uncertainty is when surprises become more frequent or larger than our model says they should be. That is the signal that the model itself is wrong, and it is thought to trigger a reset: attention widens, learning speeds up, old rules are questioned.
This is the exception monitor. The brain does not only watch what differs from its prediction. It watches how much it is being surprised overall, compared with how much it expects to be. When surprise rises above its usual level, the brain stops trusting its model and starts looking around. A dashboard should do the same.

title: What a Quiet Screen Cannot See
text:
10. Changes that leave no trace
The exception monitor has a limit too, and it is better to say it plainly. It sees changes that leave a trace in the data, even in fields the shape does not use. It cannot see changes that leave no trace in any data at all.
Suppose the copilot’s answers in Italian slowly get worse, less accurate and less useful, while staying exactly as fast. Speed telemetry will never show it. No shape, no exception and no field will move, because nothing we record is affected. The only places this shows up are people: a user who stops using the copilot, a colleague in Milan who mentions it over coffee, an engineer who reads twenty Italian answers one afternoon.
So there are three kinds of change, and each needs a different watcher (Figure 5).



Figure 5. Three kinds of change and who can see them. Changes in what the shape describes reach the dashboard. Changes elsewhere in the data reach the exception monitor. Changes that leave no record can only be seen by people.



Changes inside the shape reach the dashboard. This is what the first essay was about.
Changes in the data but outside the shape reach the exception monitor. This is what this essay adds.
Changes outside the data reach no machine. They need people who regularly look at the real thing: read the answers, visit the shop floor, talk to the users.

The third circle is not a footnote. In 1983, Lisanne Bainbridge described the “ironies of automation”: the more reliable an automatic system becomes, the less often people practise the skills they need on the day it fails. A quiet dashboard makes this worse, because it removes the daily contact with the system that used to keep people’s intuition alive. If we take away the crowded screen, we must give back that contact in a deliberate form: a regular, unhurried look at raw cases, chosen at random, by people whose job is to notice what nobody asked them to look for.

title: What a Quiet Screen Cannot See
section: 11. Proving that the system can still see
text:
11. Proving that the system can still see
There is one more trap. Even a good exception monitor can break silently. A pipeline can stop filling a field; a threshold can be set too high after a busy month; a model can be retrained in a way that hides the exceptions inside the rule. Each of these produces a quiet screen.
Engineers already know how to deal with this in other fields. Fire alarms are tested. Pilots train in simulators on failures they hope never to see. In large software systems, chaos engineering deliberately breaks things in production, in small and controlled ways, to check that the monitoring notices.
The same idea works here. From time to time, inject a small, known, artificial change into a copy of the data: make one slice of synthetic requests slower, along a dimension the shape does not track. Then check that the exception monitor notices, and how fast. If it does not, the silence of the following weeks means nothing. If it does, we have evidence, not just hope, that the system can still see.

title: What a Quiet Screen Cannot See
text:
12. A better heartbeat
Put together, the weekly heartbeat becomes a short, honest report of what was checked and how well:

Week 12. Shape checked on this week’s data: no material change. Exceptions: usual size; no recorded field explains them. Last drill: injected slowdown on a hidden slice, caught after 4 days. Last human review of raw cases: 3 weeks ago.

Each line answers a different doubt. The first says that our understanding still holds. The second says that it still fits: nothing is hiding in the leftover part. The third says that the watcher can still see. The fourth says when a person last looked at the world directly, outside every model.
This is still a very small amount to read: four lines a week instead of forty tiles a day. But now the silence carries information. It says not only “nothing changed”, but “nothing changed that we could have seen, here is how much we could see, and here is when we last checked the rest”.

title: What a Quiet Screen Cannot See
text:
13. Conclusion
The objection to the first essay was right: a system that only watches its own picture of the world cannot see what lies outside that picture, and it will often explain away what it cannot see. More tiles are not the answer; a crowded screen has blind spots too, it just hides them under noise.
The answer is to watch the part of the data the picture cannot explain. When the world moves sideways, away from what our model describes, the exceptions grow and take on a pattern long before anyone thinks of adding a new chart. Watching them is cheap, it needs no knowledge of what might go wrong, and it tells us both that our understanding has stopped fitting and roughly where.
And for what leaves no trace in any data, there is no shortcut: people have to keep looking at the real thing. An empty dashboard is the right goal. But silence is a claim, and like any claim, it has to be earned.

title: What a Quiet Screen Cannot See
text:

title: AI, Honestly
text: Latest writing

title: Fast AI
text:
Essay, October 2026. The code for the figures is here: figs.py.
In short. Experts learn slowly, once, and then act fast on habit. Most AI automation today does the opposite: an agent reasons from scratch on every run, which compounds errors, costs time and forgets what it learned. Fast AI uses the large model before the loop, as a compiler: it builds a structured memory once, and fast, explainable models run the process. The agentic loop is kept for the exceptions, and what it learns there becomes the next habit.

title: Fast AI
section: 1. Learning is slow, habits are fast
text:
1. Learning is slow, habits are fast
Think of a new accountant in their first week. Every invoice is a small investigation. They read it line by line, check the contract, look up the supplier, ask a colleague which budget it belongs to. Ten years later, the same person glances at an invoice and knows. They have not become a faster thinker. They have turned years of slow learning into fast habits.
This is how expertise works, in people and in most living things. Learning is slow and deliberate, and it happens rarely. Acting is fast and nearly automatic, and it happens constantly. The slow part builds a structure; the fast part uses it. When something truly new appears, the expert slows down again, thinks, and if the lesson is worth keeping, it becomes a new habit.



Figure 1. Schematic. The effort an expert spends on a routine case falls as slow learning turns into fast habit. When something truly new appears, the expert slows down again, and the lesson becomes the next habit.


I call this idea Fast AI. Not fast because the hardware is quick, but fast because the thinking has already been done.

title: Fast AI
section: 2. The agent that reads the manual every morning
text:
2. The agent that reads the manual every morning
Now look at how we build automation with AI today.
The typical agent receives a task, reads the context, reasons about what to do, calls a tool, reads the result, reasons again, calls another tool, and continues until it believes the task is done. It is impressive to watch. It is also an employee who arrives every morning with no memory and reads the whole manual again before touching anything.
For automation processes, this has four costs.

Errors compound. If each step is right 95% of the time, a 20-step loop gets everything right only about 36% of the time (0.95 to the power 20). Agents add checks and retries to compensate, which adds more steps, more time and more cost.
It is slow. Each step is a call to a large model that takes seconds. A process that runs ten thousand times a day pays that price ten thousand times, for reasoning that was nearly identical yesterday.
It is not repeatable. Give the same input twice and the agent may take a different path. In regulated work, the question is not only “is the answer right?” but “would it give the same answer tomorrow, and can you show me why?”. A loop of free-text reasoning is hard to audit and harder to certify.
It does not accumulate. What the agent figured out on Monday is gone on Tuesday, unless someone builds a memory around it. The intelligence is spent, not invested.




Figure 2. Errors compound. The chance that every step of a loop is right falls quickly with the number of steps. At 95% per step, a 20-step loop is fully right only 36% of the time.


None of this means agents are bad. It means they are the wrong default for work that repeats.

title: Fast AI
text:
3. Compile, don’t interpret
Programmers know this distinction well. An interpreter reads and executes a program line by line, every time it runs. A compiler reads the program once, works hard to understand and optimise it, and produces something that runs fast and identically, again and again.
An agentic loop interprets the task on every run. Fast AI compiles it.
In this view, the language model’s best role in automation is not to sit inside the loop. It is to work before the loop, as the compiler. It does the slow, intelligent work once: reading, extracting, structuring, connecting. Then it steps aside, and something fast and simple runs the process.



Figure 3. Interpret or compile. An agentic loop puts the large model inside every run. Fast AI uses it once, before the loop, to build a memory and fast models; the runs that follow are fast, identical and explainable.

title: Fast AI
section: 4. The slow part: a structured memory
text:
4. The slow part: a structured memory
What does the language model compile the domain into? My answer is a knowledge graph: a structured memory of the things in a domain and how they relate.
Language models are very good at the slow work this requires. Give them contracts, policies, past cases, emails and the notes experts leave behind, and they can extract the entities and relations hidden in all that text. For supplier invoices, that means suppliers, contracts, cost centres, approvers, products and the links between them: this supplier’s invoices go to this budget, amounts above this limit need a second approval, this kind of line item was disputed three times last year.



Figure 4. A small piece of a knowledge graph for supplier invoices. Every fact is a node or a link that a person can inspect, correct or delete. Names and values are illustrative.


Three things make the graph more valuable than a pile of documents or a long prompt.

It is explicit. Every fact is a node and a link that a person can inspect, correct or delete. Experts can validate it, and they should, because extraction makes mistakes.
It is stable. It does not change between runs unless someone changes it. The same question gets the same facts.
It accumulates. Every new case, correction and exception can be added. The intelligence is invested, not spent.

This is the slow learning of the expert, written down.

title: Fast AI
section: 5. The fast part: trees and networks together
text:
5. The fast part: trees and networks together
With the memory in place, the decision itself rarely needs a large language model. It needs the right fast model, and here Fast AI has a second meaning: it is a hybrid, not deep learning everywhere.
Deep learning is unmatched at perception: turning raw, messy inputs such as images, scanned documents, sound or free text into meaningful features. Decision trees, and especially gradient-boosted trees, are often better at deciding: taking a table of meaningful features and producing a choice. On structured, tabular data, which describes most business decisions, well-tuned tree ensembles still match or beat deep networks in careful public benchmarks, while being faster, needing less data and being far easier to explain.
So the natural split is:

Deep networks perceive. They read the scanned invoice, the photo or the text of a request, and turn it into features.
The knowledge graph remembers. It supplies what is known about those features: past cases, rules, constraints.
Trees decide. They combine both into a decision in milliseconds, and they can show which features drove it.




Figure 5. The hybrid. A deep network turns raw input into features, the knowledge graph adds what is known about them, and a tree ensemble makes the decision and shows its reasons.


Each part does what it is best at. None of them needs to think from scratch on every case.

title: Fast AI
section: 6. The loop moves to where it belongs
text:
6. The loop moves to where it belongs
Fast AI does not remove deliberation. It moves it.
The fast path handles the common cases. But every fast model should know when it is unsure: a low confidence score, a case unlike anything in its memory, a combination the graph has never seen. Those cases, and only those, go to the slow path: a language model reasoning through the problem, an agent exploring options, or a person.
And when the slow path solves a new case, the answer does not vanish. It goes back into the knowledge graph, and if it repeats, the fast models are retrained on it. Deliberation becomes habit. This is the expert again, slowing down only for the truly new, and learning from it.



Figure 6. Fast path and slow path. Familiar cases are decided in milliseconds. Unfamiliar ones go to a language model, an agent or a person; their answers return to the knowledge graph, and repeated ones are used to retrain the fast models.


So the agentic loop does not disappear. It stops running on every case and starts running on the exceptions, where its intelligence pays off.

title: Fast AI
text:
7. An example: routing supplier invoices
Take a common task in any finance department: deciding what to do with each incoming invoice. Approve it, send it to the right person, or flag it.
The agentic way. An agent receives the invoice, calls a tool to read it, reasons about the supplier, searches the contracts, reasons about the amount, looks up the approval rules, proposes a route, checks it and adjusts. It may take half a minute, cost a noticeable amount, and route slightly differently next time. Explaining why it chose this approver means reading pages of its reasoning.
The Fast AI way. Months earlier, a language model read the contracts, policies and past decisions, and built a graph of suppliers, budgets, limits and approvers. The finance team reviewed it. Now, for each new invoice, a network reads the document, the graph supplies the relevant contract and history, and a tree ensemble picks a route in milliseconds. It explains its choice: supplier, amount against contract, cost centre, past disputes. When an invoice is unlike anything seen before, it says so and hands it to a person or an agent. Their answer enriches the graph.



Figure 7. Routing supplier invoices, two ways. The agent reasons through every invoice from scratch. Fast AI does the reading once, months earlier, and then routes each invoice in milliseconds with its reasons, handing only the unfamiliar ones to a person or an agent.


Both use AI. Only one of them gets faster and better every month.

title: Fast AI
text:
8. What Fast AI costs
This approach has real costs, and they are worth stating.

The graph is work. Extraction errors must be caught, and someone has to own the memory. A wrong fact in the graph is repeated quickly and confidently, which is worse than a slow mistake.
It needs repetition. For tasks that are truly one-off or open-ended, compiling makes no sense. There is nothing to reuse, and the agent is the right tool.
The world drifts. New suppliers, new rules, new products: a fast system can go on confidently applying old habits. It needs a monitor that notices when its decisions stop fitting, as my last essay argued for dashboards.
It takes design. An agent can be set up in an afternoon. A hybrid of graph, networks and trees takes engineering. That upfront cost is precisely the slow learning, and it pays off only if the process repeats enough.

title: Fast AI
text:
9. Conclusion
We are tempted to put the most powerful model in the middle of every process, thinking on every run. For open problems, that is right. For automation, it is often like asking a senior expert to reread the whole manual before every routine job.
The alternative is older than AI. Learn slowly, once, and write down what you learned. Act fast, with simple tools you can explain. Slow down only when something is truly new, and turn what you learn there into the next habit.
Use the large model to build the memory, not to replace it. Let deep learning perceive and trees decide. Keep the loop for the exceptions. That is Fast AI: not less intelligence, but intelligence spent once and invested, instead of spent again on every run.

The views in this essay are my own and do not describe any product or plan of my employer.

title: A Universe Without a Bottom
text: Something different, just this once. This blog is usually about AI, machines and measurement. This essay is not. It is a personal detour into physics, written by someone who is neither a physicist nor a mathematician, following a question out of curiosity. Its follow-up, Decided in the Bulk, Written on the Boundary, brings the question back to AI.

title: A Universe Without a Bottom
section: It must be simpler than this
text:
It must be simpler than this
I am not a physicist. I am not a mathematician. But one evening I opened a new physics paper, Holograms and Standard Models by Miyashita, Sekino and Susskind, and tried to follow it.
I got lost quickly. Fermions, ensembles, double-scaled limits, Feynman diagrams that look like flowers. And my first reaction was simple: something is wrong here. It must be easier. I believe the universe is fundamentally simple.
This essay is what happened when I followed that feeling. I didn’t find the answer. I found better questions, and maybe that is the point.

title: A Universe Without a Bottom
text:
The surface knows everything
The first surprise came from black holes. In the 1970s, Bekenstein and Hawking found that the information a black hole can hold depends on the area of its surface, not on its volume.

S = \frac{A}{4\,\ell_P^2}

In plain words: cover the horizon with tiny tiles, each the size of the smallest length physics knows, and you have counted everything inside. Double the size of the black hole and its information grows four times, not eight.
This is strange. In everyday life a bigger box holds more things because it has more room inside. Here the inside seems to be written on the walls. Physicists call this the holographic principle: our three-dimensional world may be like an image projected from a flat surface.
So I asked myself: what if area and volume are not two different things? What if they are two faces of the same idea? It turns out physicists ask this too. Some say the area measures how much things are connected (entanglement) and the volume measures how complicated they are. Maybe space is just the shape that information takes when we look at it from inside.

title: A Universe Without a Bottom
text:
Everything from nothing
Einstein did not change physics with more complicated equations. He took one simple idea completely seriously: light moves at the same speed for everyone. So I wondered if we are looking in the wrong place. What if there is nothing at all, and that nothing is creating everything?
To my surprise, the paper I could not follow says something close to this. The authors put their model at infinite temperature. That sounds extreme, but it means something simple: every possibility is equally likely. No preference, no structure, no information. It is the state of maximum ignorance, the closest thing to “nothing” that quantum physics allows.
And from this featureless state they claim a whole small world appears: particles, forces, even the tiny energy of empty space. Their motto is “set it and forget it.” You choose one number, how big the system is, and the rest follows.
Others had similar dreams. Some physicists noticed that the energy of matter and the energy of gravity may cancel exactly, so a universe might cost nothing to make. John Wheeler said “it from bit”: reality built from yes-or-no answers, information before matter. Of course, their “nothing” still has laws of physics in it. Why there are laws at all is still a mystery.

title: A Universe Without a Bottom
text:
Grains within grains
Then another thought. What if we never reach the final piece? What if there is no end?
History points that way. We thought atoms were the bottom. Then we found the nucleus, then quarks. Each time the “fundamental” level turned out to be made of something else.
But the black hole formula seems to say no. If a region can hold only a limited amount of information, it cannot hide infinite layers inside. There must be a floor.
Unless the floor belongs only to us. What if what we call the universe is just one grain? The limit would apply inside our horizon, the part we can see, and not to everything. Some cosmologists already imagine this: space inflating forever, making bubble universes like ours, each one a grain, each with its own rules.
And it should work both ways. In 1987 physicists showed that a tiny bubble of very dense energy could grow into a new universe. From outside it would look like a small black hole that disappears. From inside it would be a whole cosmos, expanding, maybe one day full of people asking the same questions. A grain inside our grain. And maybe ours is a grain inside someone else’s.

title: A Universe Without a Bottom
text:
The vertigo
At this point I felt something I did not expect. A kind of dizziness. Nothing creating everything. Grains inside grains. No final layer. Are we at the end of thinking, or just getting close to going a bit mad?
I don’t think it is madness. Pascal, more than three hundred years ago, wrote that the eternal silence of infinite spaces frightened him. Einstein said the most incomprehensible thing about the universe is that it is comprehensible. The dizziness seems to be what you feel when you follow the questions honestly.
The hard part is not the physics. It is accepting that we may go from nothing to nothing, with no final answer waiting for us. We want an end. We tell stories with endings. We look for the cause behind the cause. Being told the chain may never close feels like losing the ground under your feet.

title: A Universe Without a Bottom
section: The meaning is in the middle
text:
The meaning is in the middle
Mathematics went through this once. In 1931 Kurt Gödel proved that mathematics can never be complete: there will always be true things it cannot prove. Many thought it was the end. It was not. Mathematics kept growing, and the open horizon became part of its beauty.
Maybe physics is the same. An end out of reach does not make the answers along the way less real. Feynman said he could live with doubt and not knowing, and that it was more interesting than having answers that might be wrong.
And “from nothing to nothing” forgets the middle. The middle is everything: stars, black holes, and someone on a quiet evening trying to understand a paper too difficult for them. If there is no final end, then asking is not a failure to arrive. Maybe it is what the universe does when it becomes complex enough to look at itself.
I started by believing the universe must be simple. I still believe it. But maybe simple does not mean finished.

title: A Universe Without a Bottom
text:
Sources

Miyashita, Sekino and Susskind, Holograms and Standard Models (2026)
Bekenstein–Hawking black hole entropy, Wikipedia
Blau, Guendelman and Guth, “Dynamics of false-vacuum bubbles”, Physical Review D 35, 1747 (1987)
Kurt Gödel, incompleteness theorems (1931)


The views in this essay are my own and do not describe any product or plan of my employer.

title: Decided in the Bulk, Written on the Boundary
text:
Essay, October 2026. A follow-up to A Universe Without a Bottom. Everything is open: download the code and results (zip, 2 MB), browse them on GitHub, or read the working paper (PDF, 4 pages).
In short. A physics paper about how structure appears out of complete disorder made me ask a question I could actually test: while an AI image generator turns noise into a picture, where does the picture’s information live, in the inside of a region or on its border? I ran the experiment in one evening, on two CPU cores, with an AI as lab partner. Finished images follow an area law: information lives on borders. But on the way, the big decisions are made across the whole image first, and only later settle onto the edges. I also found a way to measure this inside any image generator using nothing but its ability to remove noise, and checked it against exact answers. None of this is my field. The part I want to stress is how it was possible at all.

title: Decided in the Bulk, Written on the Boundary
section: 1. It must be simpler than this
text:
1. It must be simpler than this
Recently I wrote about reading a physics paper I could not follow: Holograms and Standard Models, by Miyashita, Sekino and Susskind. My first reaction was simple. Something is wrong here. It must be easier. I believe the universe is fundamentally simple.
That essay ended in philosophy. Grains inside grains, nothing creating everything, and the idea that the meaning is in the middle.
This one ends in an experiment.
I am a software architect, not a physicist. But I kept coming back to one idea from that paper, and one evening I asked a different question: could I actually test something? Not about the universe. About the AI systems I work with every day.

title: Decided in the Bulk, Written on the Boundary
text:
2. The surface knows everything
The idea that stuck is the holographic principle. In the 1970s, Bekenstein and Hawking found that the information a black hole can hold depends on the area of its surface, not on its volume. Double its size and its information grows four times, not eight.
Physicists found the same pattern elsewhere. In many systems, the information shared between a region and everything around it grows with the region’s boundary. They call it an area law. When it grows with the region’s size instead, it is a volume law.
Susskind and his colleagues go further. They build a small world of particles and forces from a system at infinite temperature, the state of maximum disorder, the closest thing to “nothing” physics allows. Structure from nothing, organised on a surface.
I could not check their mathematics. But their question felt general: when structure appears out of complete disorder, where does its information live?

title: Decided in the Bulk, Written on the Boundary
section: 3. A machine that builds structure from disorder
text:
3. A machine that builds structure from disorder
Then I realised I already knew a machine that builds structure from disorder.
Image generators like Stable Diffusion are diffusion models. They start from pure random noise, the same maximum-disorder state, and remove the noise step by step until an image appears. A face, a cat, a handwritten digit.
The universe gives us one run, seen from inside, mostly through a horizon. A diffusion model gives us as many runs as we want, and we can stop it at any moment and look.
So the question became concrete. While an image forms out of noise, does the information shared between a patch of the image and the rest of it grow with the patch’s border, or with its size? Area or volume? And does that change along the way?

title: Decided in the Bulk, Written on the Boundary
text:
4. What I measured
The measurement is simple to state. Take a square patch of an image. Ask how much knowing the rest of the image tells you about that patch. Physicists call this mutual information. Then make the patch bigger and watch how that number grows.
If it grows like the border of the patch, it is an area law. If it grows like the number of pixels inside, it is a volume law. I summarise the growth with one number, β, from

I(L) \propto L^{\beta},

where L is the side of the patch in pixels: β close to 1 means area law, close to 2 means volume law.
I did not use a giant neural network. I used something I could compute exactly: a statistical model of handwritten digits (the classic MNIST dataset) built from 40 simple pieces, four per digit. It learns real structure; on images it has never seen, it is far better than a simple model. And for this kind of model, every stage between noise and finished image can be calculated precisely, with no training noise and no guessing.
The most important part is the comparison. For every measurement I also built a control: a much simpler model that has exactly the same correlations between pixels but none of the real structure. No strokes, no digits, just smooth statistical blur. Whatever the real model does that the control does not, comes from actual structure. Without that control, I would have fooled myself at least twice.

title: Decided in the Bulk, Written on the Boundary
text:
5. What I found
Finished digits follow an area law. At the end of generation, β is 1.07. The information a patch shares with the rest of the image grows with its border.
But on the way, something else happens. In the noisy early phase, the real model carries up to 2.4 times more shared information than the control, and that extra information grows more like the size of the patch than its border. As the image sharpens, the extra information moves toward the borders, and the two curves meet (Figure 1).



Figure 1. Left: digits generated by the learned model. Right: the scaling exponent β along the generation path, from heavy noise (left) to finished image (right). The real model (blue) carries extra, bulk-like information in the noisy phase, well above the control with the same pixel correlations (orange). Both converge to an area law, β = 1.07 for finished digits.


Here is how I read it. Early on, the model is deciding the big things: which digit, roughly where, which way it leans. That is a fact about the whole image, and every pixel carries a little evidence about it, so it scales with size. Later, the model draws the details: strokes, edges, where black meets white. Those are local, and they live on borders.
Or, in one line: structure is decided in the bulk and written on the boundary.

title: Decided in the Bulk, Written on the Boundary
text:
6. What did not work
I expected a sudden switch, like water turning to ice, at one precise moment. A first coarse run seemed to show one. When I repeated it with eleven noise levels and three independent runs, the jump disappeared. The change is smooth (Figure 2). The “sudden switch” was noise in a single run.



Figure 2. The same measurement on a fine grid of noise levels, repeated three times with independent model fits and samples (bars: ±2 standard deviations). a. The total information converges smoothly to an area law; there is no sudden jump. b. The part that comes from real structure, beyond the control, starts close to a volume law and moves toward an area law as the image sharpens.


I keep it in the story because it is exactly the kind of mistake that is easy to publish and hard to take back.

title: Decided in the Bulk, Written on the Boundary
text:
7. What it does not show
I asked for a tough review of my own results, the kind a referee would write. Here is what holds up less well than I would like.

The area law alone is not surprising. Any image whose pixels mostly correlate with their neighbours gives an area law. Physicists have known this for years. The new part is not the final area law but the extra structure and how it moves from bulk to boundary.
It describes the data, not the network. Because I computed everything exactly, the results describe what noisy digits look like at each stage, which is the same for any perfect generator. To say how real neural networks behave, I need to test a trained one.
The images are tiny. At 28×28 pixels I can only compare patches from 2 to 12 pixels wide. That is less than one order of magnitude, and the blank border of each digit distorts larger patches.
The physics is an analogy. A black hole’s surface and the border of an image patch are not the same thing. The parallel is suggestive, and testable, but it is not a proof of anything about the universe.

None of this makes the work worthless. It tells me exactly what to do next.

title: Decided in the Bulk, Written on the Boundary
text:
8. Seeing inside any generator
The second limitation bothered me most. My exact method only works on simple models. Real generators, the ones people actually use, are giant neural networks where nothing can be computed exactly.
Then I came across a result from information theory, from 2005, by Guo, Shamai and Verdú. It links information to how hard it is to remove noise. Applied to my question, it says something I find beautiful:

The information a patch shares with the rest of the image equals how much seeing the rest helps you clean up that patch, added up over all noise levels.

In symbols, with A the patch, B the rest of the image and \text{mmse} the error of the best possible denoiser at a given signal-to-noise ratio \gamma:

I(A;B) = \frac{1}{2}\int_0^{\text{snr}} \Big[\, \text{mmse}_A(\gamma) + \text{mmse}_B(\gamma) - \text{mmse}_{A \cup B}(\gamma) \,\Big]\, d\gamma

That matters because cleaning up noise is exactly what a diffusion model is trained to do. So in principle you could measure the information map of any generator just by asking it to denoise a patch twice: once seeing only the patch, once seeing the whole image.
I tested this on my digit model, where I already knew the exact answer. The two routes agree, with a median difference of 3% across 32 comparisons (patch sizes from 2 to 12 pixels, noise levels from heavy to light). The largest difference was 14%, on one very small, very noisy patch (Figure 3).



Figure 3. Information measured from denoising errors alone (vertical) against the exact value (horizontal), for 32 combinations of patch size and noise level. Points on the dashed line agree perfectly. The median difference is 3.1%.


This is the part I find most valuable. The exact calculations become a ground truth to check a method that can scale to real models. The next step is to run it on a trained neural network. That needs a model that can denoise with part of the image hidden, which many image generators already can.

title: Decided in the Bulk, Written on the Boundary
section: 9. You don’t need a big machine
text:
9. You don’t need a big machine
Everything in this essay ran on two CPU cores. No GPU, no cloud cluster, no downloaded giant model. The longest run took about seven minutes.
At one point I was told the next step needed a GPU. I pushed back: why should a question need a big machine? It turned out the honest answer was that only one specific claim needs it, the one about trained neural networks. Everything else, the exact calculations, the controls, the repeated runs, fits on a laptop. Some of the best physics ever done was tabletop physics. A well-controlled small experiment beats a sloppy big one.

title: Decided in the Bulk, Written on the Boundary
section: 10. A lab partner, not an oracle
text:
10. A lab partner, not an oracle
I should be transparent about how this was done. I did it in one evening with Claude, Anthropic’s AI, as a lab partner. I brought the questions and the stubbornness; it wrote and ran the code, searched the literature, and, importantly, reviewed the results harshly when I asked it to. It also caught its own mistakes: a model that looked better than it was, a chart label that overstated a result, a “sudden transition” that was not there.
Look back at the path of this essay and count the steps that would have stopped me alone:

From a feeling to a measurable question. “It must be simpler” is not a hypothesis. Turning it into “does mutual information scale with the border or the size, and does that change along the generation path?” took a conversation, not a degree.
From a question to code that runs. Exact mutual information for a 784-pixel mixture model, Monte Carlo estimates with error bars, a fair control. Each is a week of reading for an outsider. Here, each was a script I could read, run and question within minutes.
From a result to a result I trust. The control model, the three independent runs, the fine grid of noise levels: these exist because I kept asking “how would I fool myself here?”, and the answers came back as experiments, not opinions.
From a dead end to a way forward. The method that works on real generators comes from a 2005 information-theory paper I had never heard of. Finding it, understanding what it says about my question, and testing it against the exact values all happened in the same evening.
From a claim to a smaller, honest claim. The harsh review took the area law off its pedestal and left the more interesting part standing. The GPU question turned “this needs a big machine” into “only this one claim does”.

None of these steps is new science on its own. What is new, for me, is that they can follow each other at the speed of curiosity. The distance between “I wonder whether…” and “here is the plot, here is the control, here is why it might be wrong” used to be months, and for someone outside the field it was usually infinite. That evening it was hours.

title: Decided in the Bulk, Written on the Boundary
text:
11. Innovation is in the asking
This is the part of AI I find most interesting. Not that it answers, but that it lets someone like me ask properly: run the experiment, check it, and throw away what does not hold.
It is tempting to say that AI will produce new ideas by itself. I do not think that is what happened here. The question came from me, reading a paper I could not follow and refusing to let it go. The direction changed three times because of judgement calls: insist on a control, distrust a jump that looked too good, refuse to accept that a question needs a big machine. What the AI removed was the cost of each step in between. When trying an idea costs minutes instead of weeks, you try more of them, you kill the bad ones sooner, and the good ones get pushed further than you would ever have pushed them alone.
That also changes what rigour means for an outsider. The danger of a fast partner is that you go fast in the wrong direction, and a confident AI can make a wrong result look finished. The defence is the same as in any lab: controls, repeated runs, a referee who is paid to be unkind, and everything published so that others can check. The AI can play the referee too, if you ask it to. You have to ask.

title: Decided in the Bulk, Written on the Boundary
text:
12. A very good middle
I started with a feeling: the universe must be simpler than that paper. I still believe it. But I see now that simple does not mean easy, and it does not mean finished.
In my last essay I wrote that “from nothing to nothing” forgets the middle, and that the middle is everything. This experiment is a small version of that idea. A machine starts from noise, from nothing. It ends with a digit, a finished thing. And in between, there is a moment where the big decisions are made everywhere at once, before they settle quietly onto the edges.
I don’t know if the universe works like that. I do know that a question asked on a quiet evening can become something you can measure. That is not the end of anything. It is a very good middle.

title: Decided in the Bulk, Written on the Boundary
text:
13. Try it yourself
Everything is open. You can rerun every number and every figure in this essay on an ordinary laptop in about half an hour.

Code and results: download as a zip, or browse on GitHub. It contains all scripts, the result files, the figures, and a run_all.sh that reproduces everything. The only thing to download is the MNIST dataset (about 11 MB); the README gives the link. MIT licence.
Working paper: From Noise to Boundaries: Area-Law Information Scaling Along the Diffusion Path, a four-page technical version with the equations and references.
Requirements: Python with NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn and Matplotlib. No GPU.

If you work on diffusion models, information theory or the physics of learning, I would love your critique, especially on the denoising-error method and how to test it on a trained network. And if you are, like me, someone outside the field with a question that will not leave you alone: try it. You may not need a bigger machine. You may just need a smaller experiment, and a good partner to run it with.
